JSON: Name: gut_methanotroph_pipeline Title: Experimental and computational pipeline to evaluate human-derived gut methanotroph colonization as a methane-reduction intervention to modulate intestinal transit and host fat metabolism Short Hypothesis: Oral colonization with a viable human-derived methanotroph strain reduces intestinal methane concentration, which causally increases intestinal transit speed and decreases intestinal lipid uptake and adiposity-related outcomes in a mammalian host. Related Work: Existing work has characterized methanogenic archaea in the gut and associated elevated methane with slower intestinal transit and altered metabolic phenotypes; clinical and experimental approaches to reduce methane have included broad-spectrum antibiotics, breath testing for diagnosis, and symptomatic management. Environmental and engineered methanotroph research details methane-oxidation biochemistry (pMMO and sMMO) and ecological niches, but cultivation and functional testing of human-derived gut methanotrophs are sparse. Metagenomic surveys have occasionally detected methane-oxidation genes but detection is inconsistent due to low organismal abundance and variable sequencing depth. Prior interventional studies have not established direct causal chains from methanotroph colonization to methane level reduction to host physiological changes, nor have they systematically assessed genome-resolved traits of human-derived methanotroph isolates or their prevalence across cohorts. Limitations of current methods include low sensitivity for rare taxa in shallow metagenomes, a lack of validated human-derived methanotroph isolates, unclear oxygen-dependence of gut methane oxidation, and incomplete linkage between microbial gene abundance and host phenotype. Abstract: Gut-derived methane is associated with slowed intestinal transit and altered host fat metabolism, but the potential for methane-consuming bacteria (methanotrophs) native to the human gut to reduce methane and thereby modify host physiology is underexplored. We present an integrated experimental and computational pipeline to (1) isolate and genome-characterize human-derived gut methanotrophs, (2) quantify their methane-oxidation capacity in vitro, (3) test causal effects of oral colonization on intestinal methane concentration, motility, and host lipid metabolism in a mouse challenge model, and (4) survey global human metagenomes for methane-oxidation gene prevalence and disease associations. Main contributions are a reproducible culturing and genomic-analysis workflow for gut methanotrophs, standardized in vivo protocols and endpoints to test mechanistic causality, and a metagenomic mapping approach optimized for low-abundance methane-oxidation genes. Expected outcomes include validation of strain-level methane consumption, demonstration of physiological modulation of transit and fat-handling in vivo, and estimates of methanotroph gene prevalence across populations to assess translational potential. Experiments: 1) Strain isolation and genomic characterization - Source material: fecal samples from 10 healthy adult donors. - Culturing: serial enrichment in NMS1 medium with methane as sole carbon source; colony isolation on NMS1 agar under methane atmosphere. Validate axenic cultures by growth on complex media (no growth), 16S rRNA Sanger sequencing, and electron microscopy. - Sequencing: Illumina short reads (≥100× coverage) and PacBio HiFi long reads; assemble with Unicycler/Circlator; annotate pmoA/pmoB/pmoC and mmo operons. Report ANI vs reference genomes. - In vitro methane oxidation: headspace methane measurement by mid-infrared analyzer and GC; report methane ppm reduction rate (ppm·h−1) for live vs heat-killed cells; n=4 biological replicates. 2) Mouse intervention model (causal test) - Animals: male C57BL/6, 8-week-old, n=10 per group. - Groups: (A) PBS+air control; (B) methane challenge (oral methane-rich saline) alone; (C) methane + viable gut methanotroph (gavage of cultured strain); (D) methane + heat-killed methanotroph; (E) methane + non-methanotrophic control bacterium (e.g., Methylorubrum); (F) diet challenge subset: high-fat/high-sugar (HFS) + methane; (G) HFS + methane + viable methanotroph. Interventions administered twice daily for 4 weeks where applicable. - Primary endpoints: exhaled methane concentration (ppm, mid-IR) at baseline and weekly; whole-gut transit time (carmine red marker; minutes); small-intestine transit distance and rate (Indian ink method; cm/min); fecal water content (%), fecal methane headspace (ppm). - Secondary endpoints: adipose depot weights (eWAT, mWAT, ingWAT, BAT, grams), adipocyte cross-sectional area (H&E image analysis), blood lipids (TC, HDL, LDL, TG, standard enzymatic assays), fasting glucose (glucometer). - Molecular endpoints: ileal transcriptomics (RNA-seq, n=5 per group) differential expression (DESeq2) focusing on 'fat digestion and absorption' genes (Fabp1, Cd36, Apoa4, Clps, Pla2g3); qPCR for Fabp1 normalized to ACTB; ileal Pla2g3 by qPCR and/or protein assay. - Microbiome endpoints: shotgun metagenomics of feces (Illumina PE150, target ≥10 Gbp/sample); compute alpha diversity (Shannon), beta diversity (Bray-Curtis), relative abundance of methanotroph genome by read mapping (CoverM) and pmoA qPCR copies per g feces. - In vitro organ bath: ileal/colonic segments from mice and rats; gas conditions: control (20% O2/80% N2), CH4-saturation, CH4+sourced live methanotroph headspace; measure spontaneous contractile frequency and amplitude (isometric force transducers); n≥6 per condition. - Statistics: ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for multiple groups; Mann-Whitney for nonparametric endpoints; adjust p-values with Benjamini-Hochberg; report effect sizes and 95% CI. 3) Metagenomic survey and classification - Datasets: global fecal metagenomes, minimum sample sets: (i) 550 geographically diverse samples for prevalence analysis, (ii) cohort compendium of 1200+ public metagenomes annotated for health status (healthy n~500, obesity n~475, constipation n~232). - Database construction: compile methane-oxidation genes (pmoA/B/C, mmo operon) and clustered representative sequences (90% identity); build pseudo-MOG set to screen false positives. - Mapping: map filtered reads with DIAMOND (e-value <1e-3), require coverage thresholds (≥80% query coverage) and report mapped reads per million (RPM) for MOGs; subsample sequencing depth to test detection sensitivity. - Analyses: prevalence (% samples with ≥1, ≥5, ≥10 MOG reads); correlation with sequencing depth (Spearman rho); association tests between MOG abundance and BMI (Spearman), fecal consistency (ordinal regression); classifier: random forest using MOG abundance to distinguish obesity vs healthy and constipation vs healthy, report ROC AUC, sensitivity, specificity using 5-fold cross-validation. 4) Ablation and controls - Ablation 1: viable vs heat-killed methanotroph to test metabolic activity necessity. - Ablation 2: oxygen availability modulation in vivo (mucosal oxygen probes or use of microaerophilic preconditioning) and in vitro organ bath gas composition to test oxygen dependence. - Ablation 3: sequencing depth subsampling (1 Gbp to 10 Gbp) to quantify detection limits. 5) Replication and reproducibility - Minimum biological replicates per group as specified; deposit raw sequencing data and isolate genome assemblies; provide analysis scripts and MOG database. Evaluation metrics: methane ppm reduction (absolute and %), transit time (minutes), small-intestine transit rate (cm/min), adipose mass (g) and adipocyte size (μm2), blood lipid concentrations (mg/dL), differential gene expression (log2 fold-change and adjusted p-value), microbiome alpha diversity (Shannon), mapped MOG RPM, AUC for classification tasks. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Low-abundance detection: gut methanotrophs may be below detection limits in many metagenomes; sequencing depth requirements will bias prevalence estimates and increase false negatives. 2) Colonization failure: cultured human-derived strains may not stably colonize the murine gut or human gut due to host specificity, niche competition, or oxygen microenvironment mismatch. 3) Oxygen dependence: methane oxidation requires oxygen or microaerophilic niches; in vivo activity may be transient or limited to mucosal surfaces, complicating causal interpretation. 4) Ecological perturbation and off-target effects: introducing live strains may alter community structure in ways independent of methane consumption and confound phenotype attribution. 5) Model limitations: mouse physiology, diet, and microbiome differ from humans; observed effects in mice may not generalize to human clinical outcomes. 6) Measurement accuracy: gas measurements (exhaled and headspace) may be affected by sampling timing and chamber leakage; small changes may be within instrument error. 7) Genomic ambiguity: pmo/mmo gene homology with non-methanotrophic monooxygenases may generate false positives in metagenomic mapping. 8) Statistical power and cohort heterogeneity: effect sizes may be modest requiring large sample sizes; public cohort metadata heterogeneity (diet, medication, sequencing protocols) may confound association analyses. 9) Biosafety and regulatory constraints: deploying cultured live strains for translational use requires additional safety and regulatory assessment not covered by the pipeline.
